sections.title: Introduction

summary.text: Introduces the public health, antimicrobial resistance, and socioeconomic threats posed by substandard and falsified medical products, states the agreed WHO/Member State definitions, explains how supply chain complexity and procurement pressures increase risk in LMICs, and highlights the role of risk-based post-market surveillance (Rb-PMS) and NMRAs.

sections.extract: # Introduction Substandard and falsified medical products pose a multilayered threat to the stability of health systems. They endanger health, through either therapeutic failure or adverse effects, and they undermine public trust in health care. They also risk jeopardizing global efforts working to suppress antimicrobial resistance, threatening the long-term efficacy of key life-saving medicines. Further to their

sections.title: Reporting of substandard and falsified medical products

summary.text: Explains how reporting suspected substandard and falsified medical products enables NMRA investigation, market removal, and global surveillance via the WHO Global Surveillance and Monitoring System (GSMS), notes the frontline role and under-reporting of health care professionals, and motivates transitioning from paper-based reporting to standards-based digital solutions such as smartphone applications piloted in Indonesia and the United Republic of Tanzania.

sections.extract: ## Reporting of substandard and falsified medical products Reporting suspected substandard and falsified medical products allows NMRAs to investigate them more thoroughly than the reporter. When a case of a substandard and falsified medical product is confirmed, relevant authorities can quickly remove the product from the supply chain and market, impose sanctions and address system weaknesses. In the long term, this

sections.extract: ## How to use this handbook This handbook provides guidance to countries on how to adopt digital solutions for reporting of substandard and falsified medical products. sections.title: How this handbook was developed

summary.text: Describes the development of the handbook through global consultations with health care professionals, NMRAs, and Member States, pilot implementations in Indonesia and the United Republic of Tanzania, and alignment with the Principles for Digital Development, DIIG, and the WHO/ITU National eHealth strategy toolkit.

sections.extract: ## How this handbook was developed This handbook draws on the knowledge of health care professionals and NMRAs globally and has collated the lessons learned from their experiences. It builds on insights from a pilot phase, benchmarking exercises with national authorities, consultations with Member States on substandard and falsified medical product reporting barriers, public feedback on a drafted version of the

sections.title: Assess the current state and enabling environment

summary.text: Chapter 1 opener outlining the inputs, outputs (situational analysis report and stakeholder matrix), and reference resources required to assess the current state and enabling environment before implementing a digital reporting system.

sections.extract: # 1. Assess the current state and enabling environment A comprehensive assessment of the current state and the enabling environment is necessary before implementing a digital reporting system for substandard and falsified medical products. This chapter outlines the areas that should be analysed and the factors to consider. The inputs needed to inform this step and the anticipated outputs of this phase are listed

sections.title: Analyse key stakeholders

summary.text: Guides stakeholder identification and analysis across government, health care providers, funders, industry, implementers, and civil society, and presents Table 2 with sample stakeholder analysis questions across six dimensions (roles and responsibilities, information flows, influence and power, interests and expectations, engagement and collaboration, and capacity and resources).

sections.extract: ## 1.1 Analyse key stakeholders To implement an effective digital substandard and falsified reporting solution, it is essential to identify and analyse stakeholders. Stakeholders include government officials, health care providers, funding organizations, the medical product industry, technology vendors and implementers, civil society and other partners. sections.title: Assess the digital readiness

summary.text: Outlines the six areas of a country digital readiness assessment (national digital health strategy, enabling policy and regulatory environment, governance framework, human resources, technology infrastructure, and security and privacy protection) and presents Table 3 on assessing network coverage, hardware/software availability, infrastructure, security, privacy, and data ownership.

sections.extract: ## 1.2 Assess the digital readiness Different levels of preparedness for deploying digital technologies will influence the design, implementation and adoption of reporting apps. As one of the first steps, a digital readiness assessment should be conducted to ensure solutions are tailored to the existing infrastructure, capacity and context. The outputs from the assessment should inform the necessary resources,

sections.title: Assess current substandard and falsified reporting practices

summary.text: Provides guidance on evaluating current substandard and falsified reporting practices, data collection forms, digital tools, and reporting barriers, presenting Table 4 (assessing pharmacovigilance and SF reporting practices and data usage), Table 5 (common challenges and barriers across seven categories with potential solutions, including anonymous reporting considerations), and the Chapter 1 checklist.

sections.extract: ## 1.3 Assess current substandard and falsified reporting practices **Current practices.** Conduct an analysis of current practices, challenges and barriers faced in reporting substandard and falsified medical products. sections.title: Establish a shared understanding and governance framework

summary.text: Chapter 2 opener summarizing the inputs, outputs (new/amended regulatory policies, governance structures, and strategic goals), and resources for establishing a shared understanding and governance framework.

sections.extract: # 2. Establish a shared understanding and governance framework Implementing digital reporting systems requires more than just technology. It calls for a clear, strategic and participatory approach that aligns regulatory policy, governance and leadership. This section explores how countries can establish a shared understanding of the challenges and opportunities surrounding substandard and falsified medical products

sections.title: Review regulatory policies for substandard and falsified medical products reporting

summary.text: Guides the review of national regulatory frameworks supporting digital reporting of substandard and falsified medical products, covering pharmacovigilance and quality surveillance integration, mandatory and voluntary reporting obligations, and enforcement mechanisms.

sections.extract: ## 2.1 Review regulatory policies for substandard and falsified medical products reporting The regulatory framework is the backbone for any substandard and falsified medical products reporting system, shaping data flow, privacy, liability and enforcement mechanisms. Before implementing a digital reporting system, countries should evaluate existing regulatory policies, identify gaps and determine whether new

sections.title: Align policy with stakeholders

summary.text: Describes multisectoral policy alignment across law enforcement and customs, health financing and procurement agencies, innovation and ICT ministries, and regional and global regulatory authorities.

sections.extract: ## 2.2 Align policy with stakeholders Tackling substandard and falsified medical products requires more than a single institution. Effective policy depends on multisectoral collaboration across: - **Law enforcement and customs.** Align policies to enable swift data sharing with customs officers and law enforcement, who often spearhead investigations and border control. - **Health financing and procurement

sections.title: Establish governance and leadership

summary.text: Defines a three-tier governance structure (national steering committee, technical working group, and advisory council) and key leadership roles (ministry of health/NMRA, project champion, and digital health coordinator/project manager).

sections.extract: ## 2.3 Establish governance and leadership Establish a robust governance structure for coordinating the multiple stakeholders involved in substandard and falsified medical product reporting. Define clear roles and responsibilities to avoid duplication of effort, enhance transparency and create a stable platform for decision-making. sections.title: Set the strategic goals

summary.text: Explains how to set SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) strategic goals for the substandard and falsified medical product reporting application.

sections.extract: ## 2.4 Set the strategic goals Define strategic goals for the substandard and falsified reporting application so that it is built to appropriately address prioritized needs. sections.title: Analyse and mitigate risk

summary.text: Categorizes technical, financial, and political/stakeholder risks in digital transformation, references the risk management template in Annex 7, and concludes Chapter 2 with the end-of-chapter checklist.

sections.extract: ## 2.5 Analyse and mitigate risk Digital transformations often face multiple risks – technical, financial or political. Conduct a risk analysis early in the strategic planning process to allow for appropriate mitigation measures to be put in place. Examples of risk include: - **Technical risks.** System failures, cybersecurity threats, interoperability challenges. - **Financial risks.** Funding shortfalls, changes

sections.title: Define the future state

summary.text: Chapter 3 opener detailing the inputs, outputs (digital investment roadmap and new or revised digital health enterprise architecture), and resources for defining the future state of the reporting solution.

sections.extract: # 3. Define the future state Building upon the previous sections, this section delves into the critical aspects of defining the future state for the reporting solution. In transitioning from identifying and establishing governance structures and regulatory policies, it becomes essential to strategically map out the envisioned state of digital transformation in substandard and falsified medical product reporting.

sections.extract: # 4. Determine the requirements It is essential to thoroughly understand how users will engage with the system, the processes they will execute, and the data they will handle within the application before proceeding with the development and implementation of the digital reporting system. summary.text: Defines user personas for skilled health care professionals and related individuals, presenting Table 7 (examples of key user personas: Doctor, Nurse, Community health worker, Laboratory technician, and Pharmacist with descriptions, alternative titles, and ISCO codes) and Table 8 (related user persona: Individual).

sections.extract: ## 4.1 Identify user personas Identify key user personas and related user personas. A user persona is a generic depiction of a relevant stakeholder or end user who would be interacting with the reporting system. Personas help identify the wants, needs and constraints of the end users. summary.text: Explains how user scenarios translate personas into practical use cases and presents Table 9 detailing typical end-to-end reporting scenarios (discovery, initial action, accessing reporting app, completing the report, submitting the report, and follow-up/feedback) across nine health care professions.

sections.extract: ## 4.2 Define user scenarios Define clear user scenarios for each identified persona (see Table 9). These scenarios help translate roles into specific, practical use cases, ensuring that solutions are tailored to local workflows, digital readiness and user capacities. sections.title: Develop an operations and continuous improvement plan

summary.text: Guides the development of an operations, continuous improvement, and sustainability plan covering stakeholder ownership, infrastructure and maintenance resources, recurring knowledge management and training, financial planning, backups and redundancy, and change management, concluding with the Chapter 6 checklist.

sections.extract: ## 6.2 Develop an operations and continuous improvement plan Develop an operations plan to sustain the ongoing operations and continuous improvement of the reporting application, ensuring its reliability and efficiency. The operations plan addresses strategies to scale the application, including expanding the user base and adding new features; as well as the maintenance and update strategy to support continued usage
